articles.title: MAGA mom's dire warning over tech guardrails as Trump puts pedal to the metal on race with China
articles.summary: Amy Kremer's Humans First organization demands AI guardrails to protect children from chatbot dangers and prevent mass displacement of American workers.
articles.body: A conservative political activist who has been deeply entrenched in right-wing politics for decades is calling on the government to implement safety guardrails on artificial intelligence (AI), especially when it comes to protecting children and ensuring that the booming technology doesn't displace American workers en masse. "If something happens with one of these companies, whether it's a child taking their own life due to suicide by manipulation with a chatbot, these companies are not required to report it to the federal government," Amy Kremer told Fox News Digital. Kremer is the chairwoman of Humans First, a gorup that advocates for government safeguards on the technology and says it gives the American people a voice in the AI conversation, rather than leaving all the power in the hands of what it calls "Big AI globalists" who have little concern for ordinary Americans. MIKE JOHNSON REJECTS AI MORATORIUM OVER CHINA THREAT AS CONSERVATIVE ACTIVIST DEMANDS GUARDRAILS "We are a grassroots organization focused on putting guardrails and safety mechanisms in place around AI technology in order to protect the American people, our children, jobs and so forth, and also to put those guardrails in place to to make sure that the people have a seat at the table and a voice in the conversation about what goes into their community," Kremer said. Kremer, who is known by the political right for her time as a Tea Party advocate and ferocious fighter for President Donald Trump's MAGA movement, mentioned the 2025 mass shooting at Florida State University, which claimed the lives of two people and injured six others, as an instance of AI gone wrong. Court documents in that case claim that the alleged shooter, Phoenix Ikner, used ChatGPT to plan aspects of the shooting. The company was sued by the wife of one of the deceased victims, and the state of Florida took the rare step of opening a criminal investigation into the company. "If a chatbot is used in planning a school shooting like what happened at Florida State University in April of 2025, they're not required to report that to the federal government," said Kremer. "The only reason we know about a number of these things that have happened is because of lawsuits that have been filed by the victims and/or their families." She argued that as a former flight attendant, she had to report every issue on an airliner to the government. And just as hospitals, pharmaceutical companies and hordes of other industries are regulated under the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), Kremer believes that AI companies should face similar scrutiny. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS QUESTION WHETHER AI’S PROMISE OUTWEIGHS ITS RISKS AI is a hotly-contested issue ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, with some Democrats looking to reign in the technology while the Trump administration hoping to keep competition and innovation flowing in the effort to win the AI race with China. But Kremer is far from a Democrat, and she wants also wants the United States to crush China in the race for technological dominance. "I want America to win this AI race, I absolutely I do. I'm America first, always have been, and we've led the world on innovation and ingenuity," she said. "But again ... I go back to, you don't have to forego safety to have innovation and ingenuity." "I'm not siding with the Democrats," Kremer said. "I am not a tech person. I'm not anti-AI. I'm not anti-technology. I'm not anti-data center." "I am a mom with common sense and I'm a conservative, and it only makes sense that guardrails are put in place," she added. After all, Kremer said, AI companies aren't partisan actors. TRUMP'S AI RACE WITH CHINA COULD BECOME THE BIGGEST MISTAKE OF OUR TIME "They don't care about Republicans, they don't care about Democrats, they don't care about Americans. At the end of the day, I think they care about their own companies and their technology, and that's what, what drives them," she said. "And so, everything with these guys I think is contractual, you know, it's not, 'these are my friends, these are the people, I have the same ideology.' It's contractual, it's what benefits them and I think that's why they've cozied up to President Trump and Republicans in this administration and Congress." In a high-stakes summit in Washington, D.C., last week, AI was a hot topic of discussing between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump, though what exactly was discussed remains under wraps. "The Trump administration’s priority is to ensure there is a booming economy so that workers have many opportunities and experience limited volatility from any short-term disruptions," a White House official told Fox News Digital. "The goal is for workers to continue to have access to high paying jobs and that workers can easily adapt to new technologies and processes." OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION As for children's safety, the official pointed Fox News Digital to its National Policy Framework on Artificial Intelligence. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That framework calls on Congress to implement a number of AI child safety measures, including empowering parents with tools to control their children's content exposure, privacy settings, content exposure and account controls. It also asks the lawmaking body to "establish commercially reasonable, privacy protective, age assurance requirements (such as parental attestation) for AI platforms and services likely to be accessed by minors," and ensure that AI platforms implement safeguards against child sexual exploitation and self-harm.

articles.title: Trump announces US will send $90 checks to 20 million seniors enrolled in Medicare
articles.summary: President Trump announced Friday his administration will pay out a total of around $2 billion in checks to over 20 million seniors to offset Medicare Part B premium costs. In an evening Truth Social post, the president said this money would be sourced from the Medicare Improvement Fund, which he called a “pointless ‘Slush Fund.’”…
articles.body:
President Trump announced Friday his administration will pay out a total of around $2 billion in checks to over 20 million seniors to offset Medicare Part B premium costs.

In an evening Truth Social post , the president said this money would be sourced from the Medicare Improvement Fund, which he called a “pointless ‘Slush Fund.’” The fund was created by Congress in 2008 to make improvements to the Medicare fee-for-service program.

“We are finally using this Fund, along with my Most Favored Nations Deals, to substantially LOWER costs for our Seniors,” he wrote in the post. “I pledged to protect and preserve Medicare and Social Security, which were on the verge of RUIN by Joe Biden, who foolishly and maliciously let tens of millions of Illegal Aliens into our Country, and we are doing just that for America’s Seniors.”

The Trump administration will make a one-time direct deposit of $90 to the over 20 million people enrolled in this program starting early this month, according to a White House fact sheet . The standard Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90 a month, according to Medicare .

This new announcement comes as the president faces a downturn in economic approval ratings ahead of the midterm elections, in which the Republican Party is fighting to maintain its control of Congress.

An Associated Press/NORC Research Center poll published Thursday found 65 percent of Americans blame Trump’s policies for rising costs of living in the country. Seventy-three percent said they disapproved of the way he has handled economic issues.

In his Friday evening post, the president also repeated a promise he made at the GOP’s midterm convention last month to distribute $5,000 checks to every U.S. adult if the GOP keeps its majority in both legislative chambers this fall.

“Because I delivered on this very important issue for the American People, they can also rest assured the highly popular $5,000 Trump Dividend will be distributed to every U.S. Citizen if, and when, the Republicans win the Midterm Elections!” he wrote.

articles.title: The price tag on the Ken Paxton rescue mission has Republicans panicking
articles.summary: Some Republicans want MAGA Inc. to take over spending in the final few weeks.
articles.body:
Republicans know they have to spend big to save Ken Paxton. They're increasingly worried MAGA Inc. won't throw down in time.

In private conversations over recent weeks, senior Hill Republicans and GOP officials have nudged President Donald Trump's team to start spending more on the Texas Senate race before it's too late, according to three people with direct knowledge of those conversations, who were granted anonymity to discuss them.

Those fears escalated after audio leaked of Paxton privately trashing Trump's midterm convention, with some worrying it could impact whether MAGA Inc. continues spending after a current wave of GOP ad bookings run out Oct. 12.

A Trump operative told POLITICO that MAGA Inc. and its affiliates are expected to spend near $45 million on direct mail, TV, and digital advertising in Texas through Oct. 12, an increase from its previous $20 million to boost Paxton. But they said the team is still assessing how much more money to send in the final weeks, in consultation with Senate Republicans and their top super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund.

The Trump operative, who like others in this article was granted anonymity to speak candidly, would not commit to any plans when asked by POLITICO.

With national Democrats starting to finally spend for their Senate nominee, James Talarico, after months of holding off, and as polling of the race tightens, Republicans expect the cost of salvaging Paxton's campaign will only skyrocket. And, they've started to panic.

"It's a five-alarm fire, no doubt," one GOP senator said. "Can we put it out? I hope so."

"This is a slow-moving car crash that we're witnessing right now," a Republican strategist in the state said. "And there's a 75% chance that the ultimate result here will be catastrophic from a GOP Senate majority standpoint."

A fourth Republican, a national operative, spoke to the urgency factor: "While it's money we shouldn't have needed to spend, it needs to be spent now," said a national GOP operative, describing the state as more winnable than North Carolina, Georgia and potentially Ohio.

Even with a massive war chest, Texas is turning into a huge money sink for the GOP that senators worry could hurt them in other tight races as they work to defend deep-red states and try to flip blue seats in Michigan and New Hampshire.

Trump himself nodded to some of the concerns at a rally just across the Texas border in Oklahoma Thursday night, saying those voters aren't the ones he's concerned about.

"We're worried about Michigan. We're worried about Texas," he told the crowd. "We're worried about a few states."The president is scheduled to visit Texas again next week for a rally in San Antonio next Wednesday.

SLF poured another $60 million into Texas on Wednesday, bringing its total expenditure there to a record-breaking $131 million. With the MAGA Inc. money and additional GOP ad reservations, the race is already on track to top $200 million from outside Republican groups hoping to save Paxton. Paxton's own campaign recently announced a $20 million ad buy — one of the largest single media investments in a Texas Senate race.

Some Republicans want MAGA Inc. to take over spending for Paxton in Texas in the final few weeks, so SLF can focus its resources elsewhere. MAGA Inc. could also funnel money into SLF's recently established Texas PAC. But, according to two people with direct knowledge of that matter, that hasn't happened.

"At some point I think the people spending that money are going to have to make hard choices and figure out where the money can have the biggest impact, and certainly Texas is the most expensive," Sen. John Cornyn, who lost to Trump-backed Paxton in the primary, recently told POLITICO .

SLF Executive Director Alex Latcham indicated to POLITICO the group will keep spending in Texas: "Senate Leadership Fund's investment through Texas PAC affirms our commitment to maintaining the Republican majority and defeating Far-Left liberals like James Talarico."

But Republicans' money concerns have been complicated by Paxton himself. A growing number of GOP senators and top operatives have been stunned by what they described as unforced errors by the Texas Senate nominee. For example, he crossed one of the brightest red lines with Trump, telling a group of donors that "everybody's numbers dropped" after the president's GOP convention in Dallas last month, according to the audio leak reported by The New York Times.

"There seems to be very little strategy there," said another Republican senator, granted anonymity to candidly discuss the race. "Sometimes, I think [Paxton] wants to lose."

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Trump, while on his way to Texas to tour a motor facility on Thursday, told reporters he hadn't talked to Paxton about his convention comments. Later, he told a crowd in Texas that "Ken Paxton was at my side more than anybody, and I have to always remember that because he can be a pain in the ass sometimes. I'll be honest."

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told reporters this week that he hadn't seen the audio of Paxton trashing Trump's convention. He acknowledged the stakes in his home state were high — and that the influx of cash is key.

"The reason that it is a serious race and a close race right now is that for several months the Democrats were massively outspending us," he said, "and I am glad now that we are seeing money invested in communicating with the voters."

The White House has attempted to reassure concerned senators, with chief of staff Susie Wiles telling Senate Republicans this week that there will be enough money available for competitive races in the final stretch, according to two people with knowledge of the meeting.

GOP operatives in both Michigan and New Hampshire said they feel that some of the cash being shoveled toward Texas should be going to their states instead. Most polls show Republicans running narrowly behind or neck and neck in both states, even though they hold a spending advantage on the airwaves there.

"We're focusing so much on 'we've got to put this money into Texas.' Why? We've never had a problem in Texas. Let's focus on taking back a seat we haven't had in years," said an ally of former Sen. John E. Sununu, who's in a tight race against Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas. "There are real chances in Michigan and New Hampshire," said the person, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the dynamics.

Sununu's campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Latcham, who heads SLF, said that "Texas PAC is a dedicated effort that will not take resources from our other ongoing investments across the Senate map."

Recent polling still shows the Texas Senate race with a razor-thin margin. Most public polling over the past two months shows Talarico with an edge, though Paxton's campaign released an internal poll Tuesday that shows Paxton leading by three points among likely voters, 48% to 45%.

"I don't think the needle has moved in the last month," said one Texas Republican elected official, granted anonymity to speak frankly. "Unless it's the worst polling that's ever been done in political history, all this spend hasn't changed anything, and I think people have made their mind up."

Lisa Kashinsky, Samuel Benson, Alex Gangitano and Kelsey Brugger contributed to this report.

articles.title: DHS exposes dilemma behind SCOTUS deportation fight: ‘We have two choices’
articles.summary: DHS General Counsel James Percival defends third-country removals on social media as the Supreme Court temporarily stays a lower-court ruling.
articles.body: The Supreme Court temporarily cleared the Trump administration to continue its third-country deportation policy this week, as DHS’ top lawyer mounts a public defense of an immigration authority the administration says previous presidents largely left dormant. DHS has increasingly used so-called "third-country" removals when a removable alien cannot be returned to their home country or that country refuses to take them back — part of what agency General Counsel James Percival describes as a broader Trump strategy of reviving immigration authorities already on the books. "Imagine going to a country and saying, hey, we've got a guy, he's not your guy, and he's a rapist, but can he please live there?" Percival told Fox News Digital. "That's not an easy ask. It requires significant diplomatic energy… Norway is not taking a rapist from Cuba." TRUMP’S SPECIAL STRATEGY TO DEPORT ILLEGALS GIVES HIM ANOTHER TOOL FOR ENFORCEMENT The justices on Tuesday stayed a lower-court judgment restricting DHS’s policy, allowing the administration’s guidance to remain in effect while the Court considers the case on the merits. Arguments are set for December over whether agency procedures comply with federal immigration law, due process and safeguards against torture. The case does not squarely challenge DHS’s underlying authority to conduct third-country removals, but rather the procedures it must follow beforehand. "It’s in the statute expressly that we can do this," he said. "If you go back and read most of the immigration laws, there's a lot of really good tools in there that people just haven't used." The third-country provision was included in a major immigration reform package passed by Congress and signed by President Bill Clinton in 1996: the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA). "A lot of people in government sort of treat their authority like fine china," Percival remarked. "They're afraid if they ever actually use it, someone will take it away. And if you've ever owned fine china, it's like you can find yourself at the end of your life and you were so afraid you would break it you never used it." TRUMP’S FIGHT OVER RARELY USED 18TH-CENTURY DEPORTATION LAW LIVES ON IN LATEST COURT CLASH But Percival’s strategy has not come without blowback from human rights advocates, who pointed most recently to allegations that deportees were beaten by authorities in Equatorial Guinea, a tiny nation on Africa’s Atlantic coast that has been under the control of President Teodoro Obiang since 1979. Obiang's government received $7.5 million from Washington as part of an agreement with Malabo to accept third-country deportations. "I’d rather live in the United States than Equatorial Guinea too, but I’m an American citizen and I haven’t killed anybody," Percival said. The detention issue traces in part to the Supreme Court’s 2001 decision in a case involving a stateless legal resident whom the government ordered deported due to his criminal record. Kestutis Zadvydas was born to Lithuanian parents in a German displaced- persons camp, but neither Lithuania nor Germany would accept him. The court held that six months of post-removal detention is presumptively reasonable, after which continued detention can be challenged if removal is not reasonably foreseeable. Percival is making that case publicly through his "Daily Deportee" series on X, highlighting criminal deportees whose home countries will not accept them. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "If the person is a child rapist and serves 20 years, we have two choices: Find a third country — or let the child rapist go live in an American community," he said, adding that the effort is intended to shape public understanding of the issue and highlight its stakes. Percival cited Burmese national Kyaw Mya, whose home country won’t take him back. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Percival said another case he plans to feature involves a migrant who committed a violent crime, was not removed by the Bush administration after serving time and then allegedly reoffended after his release: "[He] tried to kill somebody, the gun misfired, so he pistol-whipped them instead. He served time for that. He got out," Percival explained. As DHS continues seeking to use underutilized tools in the IIRIRA and other laws, Percival pointed illegal immigrants and criminal resident aliens to another oft-repeated option that Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin continues to keep on the table: "It’s not too late to get $3,000 and a flight home."

articles.title: The Senate has remembered America’s October 7th victims. Now it’s time to heal
articles.summary: The father of a soldier killed at Nahal Oz on October 7 urges Congress to act after the Senate unanimously honored all 46 American Hamas victims.
articles.body: On October 7, 2023, my son Itay was nineteen, an American-Israeli soldier stationed at Nahal Oz protecting the border, when Hamas terrorists kidnapped and murdered him. They held his remains in Gaza for 760 days — deliberate, unimaginable psychological warfare against my family — before he was finally returned home in November 2025, the last American hostage. He was my son. He was an American. Most of his own country never learned his name, or the names of Judy Weinstein, Danielle Waldman or Carol Siman Tov. That is why it was so meaningful that the U.S. Senate unanimously passed a bipartisan resolution, led by Senators Rick Scott and Jacky Rosen, honoring the 46 Americans murdered by Hamas during the October 7 war. For the first time, their names are written into the official record of the United States Senate. The resolution reaffirms America’s commitment to seek legal justice on behalf of our families, and it will be delivered to each of us by the Secretary of State. Washington is finally stopping to remember. Families of the fallen will soon gather in the nation’s capital for "Honoring American Victims of Hamas Since October 7," the first time the U.S. government will formally recognize, in one room, its own citizens killed in the October 7 war. I have advocated for this day because most Americans have no idea their country endured one of the deadliest days of terrorism against its own citizens since September 11. MY SON WAS ONE OF 46 AMERICANS MURDERED BY HAMAS. WE NEED A US INVESTIGATION I am deeply grateful to Secretary of State Marco Rubio for stepping forward to host this memorial, and to the Howard and Allison Lutnick Foundation for their support. Together with the Senate’s vote, it tells grieving families something we have waited three years to hear: Washington sees us. These were not foreign casualties in someone else’s war. They were American sons, daughters and grandparents, murdered by extremists. But what worries me most is this: a resolution and a ceremony must not become a "check the box" moment, after which Washington moves on. Acknowledgment is not healing. Recognition is not recovery. Our families need their country to act long after the cameras leave the room. So I am asking Washington for three things. First, pass the October 7th American Victims Family Support and Remembrance Act. It would give our families — most of whom live outside the United States — the same mental health support and medical rehabilitation Congress built for 9/11 families through the Zadroga Act, and authorize a permanent memorial to the fallen here in Washington. Grief without support is grief carried alone. Second, Congress must establish a formal committee to investigate how nearly 50 of its own citizens came to be killed on October 7. This is not only about accountability — it is part of our families’ recovery. You cannot fully rehabilitate what you cannot explain, and three years later, our families still do not know how their loved ones were killed. Four Americans died in Benghazi and Congress ran eight investigations; nineteen died at Khobar Towers and the House investigated. Congress cannot defer to the Israeli government on understanding how its own citizens were killed. It should give the American people a clear accounting of how this happened, so that we can begin to heal. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Third, turn the Senate’s words into justice. As Senator Scott said this week, America "has a duty to secure justice" for its murdered citizens. The Department of Justice must keep pursuing everyone responsible for October 7 — the killers, and those who financed, armed and enabled them — until each one faces justice. Every terrorist should know that killing an American carries severe and lasting consequences. That is not vengeance. It is deterrence, and it is what protects the next American family from becoming mine. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP This week, without a single objection, the Senate showed what any country owes its citizens killed by terrorists, and the families they left behind. I could not save my son. I can still demand that our country tell the truth about how this happened, work to prevent it from happening again, hold those responsible to account, and make sure no other American family has to search for that truth alone.

Country singer Zach Bryan wore a shirt with the words “Free Palestine” on it during a Friday concert at Gillette Stadium. This follows the stadium owner’s decision to block Macklemore from performing at the venue because of his pro-Palestine advocacy.

Last month, Macklemore said he was removed from Ed Sheeran’s tour after Robert Kraft, the owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium, told the singer he could not perform at the stadium with the rapper.

Sheeran addressed the controversy during a Sept. 19 concert in Philadelphia and called the situation in Palestine “catastrophic and unjustifiable.”

This is not the first time that Bryan has weighed in on hot-button issues.

Bryan sparked criticism last October after he posted a snippet of a song on social media that contained lyrics critical of the Trump administration’s mass U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) deportation operations.

“And ICE is gonna come, bust down your door / Try to build a house no one builds no more / But I got a telephone / Kids are all scared and all alone,” he sang.

The track, titled “Bad News,” was released earlier this year amid a massive immigration crackdown in Minneapolis, Minn. Federal agents shot and killed two people and injured a Venezuelan migrant during this operation.

Then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem criticized the song as “completely disrespectful” during an interview last October with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson.

The country artist pushed back on the criticism in an Instagram story at the time.

“This shows you how divisive a narrative can be when shoved down our throats through social media,” Bryan wrote. “This song is about how much I love this country and everyone in it more than anything.

“Everyone using this now as a weapon is only proving how devastatingly divided we all are,” he continued. “We need to find our way back.”

articles.title: SCOTUS must show oil companies they aren’t above local accountability
articles.summary: If you think people should be able to hold corporations accountable in court, you should pay attention.
articles.body:
A basic moral principle is also a rule of law: If you lie about something and your lies cause harm, you should compensate people you injured. Sounds simple, but what counts as harm, whether the lie caused it, and what compensation is appropriate can be hard questions. Judges and juries wrestle with them every day.

On the first day of its new term, the Supreme Court will hear a bold argument : that no jury can even consider these questions when the allegations concern deception by fossil fuel companies about climate change. In Suncor v. Boulder County , two oil companies will be making that case to stop a lawsuit against them. If you think people should be able to hold corporations accountable in court, you should pay attention.

For decades, oil companies have cast doubt on climate change and the idea that burning fossil fuels might be to blame. But about a decade ago, investigators uncovered a trove of documents showing the industry knew the truth since at least the 1960s.

Specifically, oil and gas executives knew their industry and products were releasing huge amounts of carbon dioxide, which was causing the atmosphere to heat to a point that it could lead to — in their words — “globally catastrophic events” by the end of this century. They knew the only “uncertainty” in this chain of events was whether they would disclose the problem or do anything to reduce the level of carbon dioxide entering the atmosphere.

States and local governments struggling with expensive and avoidable climate-related damage took notice. Dozens — including Boulder County — sued oil companies under state consumer protection and product safety laws, alleging decades of industry deception .

It’s hardly the first time that local governments have sued an industry for hurting people by hiding the truth. A generation ago, thousands successfully sued tobacco companies to recover the costs of caring for smokers who were told cigarettes were safe. More recently, all 50 states did the same to companies who hid the truth about opioids .

The fossil fuel industry desperately wants to avoid that fate. Big Oil companies are trying to stop these lawsuits — not by contesting the claims but blocking state courts from hearing them.

To be clear, the state and local government lawsuits aren’t trying to regulate things like oil wells, air pollution or the car you drive. Those topics are generally covered by federal laws and contested in federal courts. The lawsuits aim to make the oil companies that lied about the risks of their products help pay for the damages those products caused. That’s the kind of case that state courts handle all the time.

Maybe you agree with the oil companies that it’s not fair to blame them for global climate change. Maybe you think that they didn’t really deceive anyone, or that the deception didn’t cause climate change or that climate change isn’t really causing damage. But this Supreme Court case is just about whether a jury should have the chance to consider those questions.

The oil companies’ most radical argument is that abstract constitutional principles shield them from being sued in state court for deceiving people. That boils down to a policy argument that the oil industry is just too important to have to answer to local governments that are dealing with the costs of climate-related damage.

Courts are meant to rule on questions of law, not policy. So, I wasn’t surprised when the Colorado Supreme Court rejected the industry’s arguments, paving the way for an actual trial. I also wasn’t surprised when the oil companies asked the Supreme Court to review that decision. No harm in trying.

But I was surprised when the court agreed to get involved before the plaintiffs even got their day in court; it had declined to get involved in similar cases on five recent occasions. Perhaps the conservative majority is itching, as many suspect, to continue its streak of prioritizing corporations over people’s health and the environment .

And I was even more surprised at the latest plot twist: Justice Alito recused himself from Suncor just one week before oral arguments. The justice didn’t explain why he bowed out, but people had been calling on him to do so because he has financial investments in the oil industry . That leaves the remaining justices to answer questions they may never have wanted to take up. At least four justices have to vote to take up a case; we don’t know if Justice Alito provided one of them.

But even without Alito, we should all still ask the same question: If the Supreme Court gives Big Oil a hall pass, which industry will be clamoring to be next? AI companies? Pharmaceutical giants?

I hope the court does the right thing and lets this case proceed. It’s hardly the court’s last chance to consider these questions. It can always take the case up after the plaintiffs get their day in court, and after a jury has made its findings.

The rule of law works best when it’s applied to everyone equally. This case will be a good test of whether the Justices believe that.

Sambhav Sankar is senior vice president for programs at Earthjustice.

articles.title: ‘Bordering on angry’: The state of play as US midterms enter final month
articles.summary: Democrats enter final stretch with surprisingly positive outlook as Republican money seeks to stem damage.
articles.body:
Washington, DC – Democrats have the momentum; Republicans are surging in defence and cash.

That narrative has emerged ahead of the United States midterm elections in November, as races across the country enter their final stretch.

With control of the US House of Representatives and the US Senate at stake, Democrats begin October with a surprisingly rosy outlook as more congressional seats are seen as in play.

Republicans, meanwhile, appear to be in damage control, pouring millions of dollars into races once seen as secure victories while injecting more funding into a handful of marquee showdowns.

The party’s standard bearer, President Donald Trump, who has embraced the notion of the election being a referendum on his leadership, enters the final month with staggeringly low approval ratings.

The most recent Associated Press-NORC polling, released on Thursday, showed Trump with 31 percent approval, the lowest during either of his two terms. Only 26 percent of respondents approved Trump’s handling of the economy, dipping two points below his predecessor, former President Joe Biden’s lowest rating on the topic.

Surveys continue to show voters rank the economy as their top issue, with topics like gas prices, made higher by the US-Israel war with Iran, dominating their concerns. Immigration and corruption have also regularly ranked high.

“The broad stroke is that Americans are disappointed, bordering on angry that President Trump hasn’t delivered on the core promises he made when he won re-election,” according to Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the conservative Ethics and Public Policy Center in Washington, DC.

Political trackers have long projected Democrats will take control of the US House of Representatives in the November 3 vote.

Winning a majority in the 435-member chamber from Republicans would give the party renewed legislative power to assert leverage over Trump, while launching investigations into his administration’s dealings. Top Democrats have already signalled that probes into Trump’s family business dealings would be top priorities.

Two election non-partisan prediction authorities, the Cook Political Report and the University of Virginia’s Sabato’s Crystal Ball, have recently assessed that the likelihood of Democrats taking the House has only increased.

The Cook Political Report recently shifted 15 House races in the direction of Democrats, moving some considered “toss-ups” to “leans Democrat” and some previously considered “lean Republican” to “toss-ups”.

One such shift was for a Texas border district represented by Republican Monica De La Cruz. Her district was emblematic of a wider Latino shift towards Trump in 2024. Once seen as holding the advantage over her challenger, Democrat Bobby Pulido, Cook now rates her race as a “toss-up”.

All told, the political analysis clearinghouse now predicts Democrats are on track to win 5 to 15 House seats.

With 30 days left to go, “there’s much more drama in the Senate than the House races”, according to Kyle Kondik, the managing editor at Sabato’s Crystal Ball.

Once considered a pipe dream for Democrats, who need a net gain of at least four seats to win a slim majority, the 100-member chamber has moved within a more comfortable striking distance.

Unlike in the House, where every seat is up for re-election, only 35 Senate seats are up for grabs in this cycle, creating a far narrower pathway to control.

“The trajectory of the polling since Labor Day (September 7) has generally been that a bad Republican environment is just getting worse,” Kondik said, adding that “the Senate just seems to get more and more competitive as the cycle has gone on”.

To be sure, the quality of polling can vary across the country, with Kondik cautioning that gauging the political temperature of the Midwest has been particularly challenging for pollsters.

Still, in North Carolina, former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper is expected to trounce former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley in the race for a Senate seat currently held by Republicans. Top conservative donors have already begun to divert funds from the contest.

Surveys have consistently shown Democrats leading in three other races for seats currently held by Republicans: Democrat James Talarico against Republican Ken Paxton in Texas; Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown against Republican incumbent Senator John Husted in Ohio; and Democratic Mary Peltola against Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska.

Races for Republican held seats in Iowa, between Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek, and in Maine, between Republican incumbent Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, remain separated by less than one point, according to Real Clear Politics polling averages.

Democrats, meanwhile, have consistently led in polling in Senate races in Georgia, New Hampshire and Michigan for seats the party currently holds.

For Republicans, salvation could be in the spending, with this year’s race continuing a US phenomenon of small fortunes poured into politics.

All told, at least $4bn had been spent on gubernatorial and congressional midterm advertising buys as of September 17, putting the race on track to become “perhaps the most expensive midterm on record”, according to Michael Franz, co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project.

Republicans entered September with a considerable funding edge. The Republican National Committee had $125.6m on hand, with the Democratic National Committee trailing far behind with $16.9m and $17.6m in debt.

When accounting for the three major committees associated with both groups, the Republican Party had $233.4m in cash, according to a CNBC analysis, while the Democratic Party had $130.4m.

Trip Yang, a Democrat strategist based in New York City, told Al Jazeera such spending can be deployed to help boost a candidate’s name recognition or to tear down a competitor.

According to AdImpact, Republicans and their allies were set to spend $888m on advertising from mid-September to election day, with Democrats and their supporters set to spend $666m.

The firm found pro-Republican ad spending would be particularly pronounced in the key Senate races in Ohio, Texas and Michigan, outpacing Democratic spending by at least $24m in each state.

Trump’s unpopularity, Yang said, means “Republicans spending millions or hundreds of millions of dollars improving their candidates’ images by itself may not be enough”.

“If you’re a little bit handicapped because your president is so toxic, you try to spend your hundreds of millions of dollars attacking the Democrats to make it more of a food fight,” he said.

A New York Times analysis estimated by the end of August at least $1bn in so-called “dark money” had been poured into the midterms. The term refers to spending where the donor’s identity is shielded, typically through nonprofit and shell-company donations to Super PACs.

Industry groups, including those supporting Crypto, AI and online betting firms, are expected to be top spenders in key races, although their support tends to cut across partisan lines.

Trump, meanwhile, has pledged to spend between $400m and $500m from his MAGA Inc Super PAC, though it has so far spent about $15m to support Paxton’s Senate bid in Texas.

Pro-Paxton ad reservations far outpaced Talarico in September, according to AdImpact data analysed by NPR, with $94m spent compared with $30m to support the Democrat.

Trump has pledged to spend the final days before the election in non-stop campaign mode, after urging supporters during his Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, to “vote like I’m on the ballot”.

His plan to criss-cross the country for rallies underscores a “base turnout” strategy meant to energise voters already loyal to the party, according to conservative analyst Olsen.

“But the Republican problem is a persuasion problem with people in the middle,” Olsen said. “[Trump’s campaigning] might help with some turnout … but their real problem is persuasion, and it’s not something that’s going to help with that in the slightest.”

Polls have spelt trouble for Republicans when it comes to swaying independents, with a PBS News, NPR and Marist poll from September 23 showing unaffiliated voters breaking for Democrats at 57 percent compared with 32 moving towards Republicans.

The scenario has created a dilemma for some top Republican candidates over whether to break from the president on his most controversial actions, according to Lee Miringoff, the director of the Marist University Institute for Public Opinion.

Senate candidates Ashley Hinson in Iowa, Jon Husted in Ohio and Mike Rogers in Michigan all recently put daylight between themselves and Trump on the war with Iran.

One Republican House candidate, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar, has criticised Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement policies as she seeks to rally Latino voters in South Florida.

Trump, in turn, reposted a social media message calling Salazar a “backstabber”.

“You need to have, you know, something else going for you other than endorsement of Trump,” said Miringoff. “Some Republicans are starting to have self-preservation kick in because they’re concerned.”

Achieving a wide-scale shift in public opinion remains a tall order for Republicans in the final stretch of the race.

Many of the defining issues are unlikely to change before November, with Trump signalling a possible escalation with Iran following the vote as he has downplayed the prospect of short-term affordability relief.

At the same time, the US president has also not ruled out actions that rights groups say could upend voter turnout. Most recently, he refused to commit to not invoking the Insurrection Act or declaring a state of emergency surrounding the vote during an interview with Time magazine.

Miringoff said he believed that the “potential for more than just a marginal shift is there”, as he assessed some Democratic candidates have struggled to present clear visions beyond opposition to Trump.

“The result isn’t formed in concrete,” he said, “to the degree that there’s going to be a lot of money still spent.”

Analyst Olsen saw less remaining wiggle room for the party.

“Republicans have the time and the resources to change the outcome with respect to a few close Senate races,” Olsen said. “But to change direction, they would need something that would be apocal.”

articles.title: Trump thanks man who helped save Flydubai flight: ‘What a job he did, he’s a hero’

articles.body:
President Trump on Friday morning thanked the Israeli plumber, Yaniv Hayoun, who intervened after a pilot stabbed his co-pilot and attempted to crash a Flydubai flight this week.

In a video message shared on Truth Social, the president praised Hayoun, saying he “did an amazing job.”

“He’s my kind of guy,” he continued. “He can be my plumber. He can be whatever he wants to be. What a job he did. He’s a hero, and I want to just congratulate him and his family.”

Hayoun worked with three other passengers to subdue the pilot before he took control of the jet’s steering controls to stabilize the aircraft, which had descended into free fall during the attack.

The plumber, who had no formal flight training, said he relied on his knowledge from watching “Air Crash Investigation,” a TV series that presents dramatized reconstructions of real air disasters.

On Thursday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced he was nominating Hayoun and three other passengers involved in the intervention effort for the Presidential Award ​for Civilian Heroism.

“Everyone who was there in those moments, the passengers and the crew, mobilized, acted with courage, supported one another in mutual responsibility, and helped prevent a severe disaster,” Herzog wrote in a social media post translated from Hebrew.

The flight, which was en route to Tel Aviv, was diverted for an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a second air crew aboard the plane took over the controls.

Indian Airline Capt. Smit Machchhar was taken to the hospital for treatment to receive medical attention for stab wounds he sustained during the attack. His co-pilot was arrested and interrogated by Saudi authorities, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday.

Trump noted in his Friday video message that Hayoun was “a Trump fan,” referencing the plumber’s message of support for the U.S. president during a conversation with Netanyahu after the incident.

“I’m a fan of his. A big fan,” Trump said in the clip.

articles.title: Newsom slaps 25% tax on private detention centers in sweeping pushback against key Trump policy
articles.summary: Gavin Newsom signed a 25% tax on private detention centers in California, targeting every ICE facility in the state and their profits directly.
articles.body: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a bill earlier this week that would impose a 25% tax on private detention centers, a policy that would apply to all the facilities that partner with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the Golden State. "If we can’t kick out private facilities, we’ll go after their profits," Newsom said in a press release. The move, which Newsom hailed as a way to push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown and what he sees as the practice of privatizing federal enforcement, is raising concerns among immigration experts who believe the increased tax could force the government to explore alternative facilities less suited to housing detainees. It also poses questions about what would happen if all eight of ICE's detention facilities chose to suspend their operations in California. CITIZENS BANK CUTS TIES WITH ICE PRISON CONTRACTORS AFTER MONTHS OF ACTIVIST PRESSURE That’s the view of Hans von Spakovsky, senior legal fellow and an immigration expert with Advancing American Freedom, a conservative-leaning think tank. "It's very clear that there's only one purpose to this California gigantic tax increase, and that is to make sure that the federal government cannot find any private property owners, any private contractors in California that are willing to lease space to the federal government," Spakovsky said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "The alternative for the federal government is to look at all the different federal properties that the government actually owns out there, over which neither Newsom or anybody else in California can impose any kind of tax, and see if any of those federal facilities can be converted to being a detention facility." Spakovsky explained that could mean repurposing warehouses or office space. The newly minted law, AB 1633, is among 20 other bills that Newsom signed on Tuesday. In its current form, the 25% tax applies to the gross income of any private detention facility and applies to federal, state and local contract recipients. Revenue from the bill will go to a "Due Process for All Fund," designated for immigration-related services, according to the bill’s language. Now that AB 1633 has been signed into law, it will go into effect on July 1, 2028. Alongside the bill, Newsom signed a handful of other restrictions. ICE EYES $20M PURCHASE OF ELECTRIC SHOCK GLOVES AS HOCHUL WARNS OF LEGAL CONSEQUENCES "We’re also banning the Orwellian practice of using shock gloves in enforcement activity as well as further protecting access to our court system," Newsom said. "We may not be able to dictate federal immigration policy, but we can make clear that activities taking place in California will be subject to California law." Despite Newsom’s framing, Spakovsky believes the governor will affect federal immigration law enforcement by limiting the overall space it has to operate. He pointed to reporting from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that details its detention needs. He explained that the government relies on private contractors, at least partially, to avoid the costs of building their own facilities. "If you look at that report, currently ICE has about enough detention space for about sixty-six thousand aliens. Okay, that's the full size of the federal government's detention capacity," Spakovsky said. If an entire state’s private detention contractors decided the tax is too high, ICE’s overall capacity could shrink. California is home to eight ICE detention facilities, according to reporting from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). All of them are privately operated. The GEO Group, a corrections company, owns five facilities. Imperial Valley Gateway Center LLC, a local detention company, owns one more. Two more were purchased by DHS in July but are run by CoreCivic, a prison company, and have contracts through 2027 and 2029. Although the bill won’t go into effect until 2028, in Trump’s last year of his second term, Spakovsky believes that the government might begin evaluating where else it can find partnerships to meet its detention needs sooner rather than later. ICE MAKES NATIONWIDE ARRESTS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS, MURDERERS, PEDOPHILES IN HOLIDAY BLITZ "Look, if I was the federal government and I couldn't find enough federal properties in California to do this, I would then go into neighboring friendlier states that I could quickly transport aliens I've detained and I would lease and rent facilities there." "I'd go to Arizona. I'd potentially go to Nevada. I'd go to other states where they might be eager for federal government money and the increased employment from private contractors hiring people to work on these facilities." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The office of Gavin Newsom did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

articles.summary: Bihar council polls on Oct 23: RJD and Congress to clash on 4 of 8 MLC seats, exposing Grand Alliance rifts; independent also enters Tirhut teacher race.
articles.body: Patna: The RJD and Congress are set for direct fights on four of the eight Bihar legislative council seats going to polls on Oct 23, exposing differences within the Grand Alliance (GA) ahead of the elections to four teacher and four graduate constituencies.The RJD has fielded candidates on six seats, including Patna and Saran teacher constituencies and Patna, Darbhanga, Kosi and Tirhut graduate constituencies. Besides Jha from Darbhanga teacher, it has fielded Sanjay Yadav (Patna teacher), Asadullah Khan (Patna graduate), Rajni Kant Pathak (Darbhanga graduate) and Manoj Kumar Jaiswal (Kosi graduate). articles.title: Democrats edge out, neck and neck with Republicans in 5 key Senate races: Polls
articles.summary: Senate Democratic candidates are edging out or polling neck and neck with their GOP counterparts in five competitive Senate races this cycle — the latest indicator that Republicans are facing a tough midterm environment in even more traditionally redder areas, according to new surveys of the races. Polling released by The New York Times and…
articles.body:
Senate Democratic candidates are edging out or polling neck and neck with their GOP counterparts in five competitive Senate races this cycle — the latest indicator that Republicans are facing a tough midterm environment in even more traditionally redder areas, according to new surveys of the races.

Polling released by The New York Times and Siena University on Saturday found Democrats leading by 6 points in the Texas Senate race, 7 points in Alaska, 3 points in Ohio, down 1 point in Iowa and tied in Kansas.

Because the surveys in Ohio, Iowa and Kansas are within the margin of error — 4.5 points in Ohio, 4.6 points in Iowa and 4.6 points in Kansas — those races are essentially tied.

Republicans are looking to stave off losses in the Senate as Democrats look to flip traditional battleground seats in places like Maine and North Carolina, in addition to other more red-leaning states like Alaska, Texas and Iowa.

While forecasters all but expect Democrats to pick up the House, the Senate remains a toss-up as the party needs to win at least four seats to regain control of the upper chamber.

In addition to a midterm environment that’s traditionally unkind to the president’s party in power, GOP candidates are grappling with Trump’s low approval ratings, an unpopular war in Iran, a tariff war with Canada and inflation where cost of living remains a concern.

Trump’s approval ratings are low across the board in all five states — between 38 percent and 41 percent — while grappling with very high disapproval ratings, according to the Times/Siena polling. His disapproval ratings in those five states range between 55 percent and 60 percent.

The state where Trump performs the worst overall is Ohio, where voters gave him a 38 percent approval rating and 60 percent disapproval rating.

The polling sample overall showed a clear enthusiasm gap between Democrats and Republicans — 97 percent of Democrats disapproved of Trump while only 80 percent of the GOP approved of his job. Another warning sign emerges with independents, as only 27 percent approve of his job as president while 71 percent disapprove.

Another worrisome area for Republicans is Trump’s approval ratings with non-college educated white voters and non-college educated non-white voters. Among white, non-college educated voters, 50 percent approve of the president’s job while 47 percent disapprove.

Among non-white, non-college educated voters, only 29 percent approve of Trump while 68 percent disapprove.

Young voters, overall, are sour on the president. Just a fifth of voters aged between 18 and 29 years old — 21 percent — approve of the president while Trump fields a 75 percent disapproval rating from the voting bloc.

The Times/Siena polls were conducted between Sept. 21 and Oct. 1, with the full sample size including 2,946 likely voters. The overall margin of error is 2.1 points.

The Iowa poll was conducted between Sept. 22 and Oct. 1, with 606 voters surveyed; the margin of error is 4.6 points. The Ohio poll was conducted between Sept. 22 and Oct. 1 with 616 voters surveyed; the margin error is 4.5 points. The Texas poll was conducted between Sept. 21 and Sept. 30 with 615 voters surveyed; the margin of error is 4.5 points.

The Kansas poll was conducted between Sept. 22 and Sept. 30 with 605 voters surveyed; the margin of error is 4.6 points. The Alaska poll was conducted between Sept. 24 and Oct. 1 with 504 voters surveyed; the margin of error is 5.1 points.

articles.title: Check your email: Notices sent regarding $309M Amazon returns settlement
articles.summary: If you’ve returned an item you bought via Amazon over a several-year period, you may qualify for payment in a new class action settlement.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – If you’ve returned an item you bought via Amazon over a several-year period, you may qualify for payment in a new class action settlement.

Back in January, the online retail giant agreed to pay $309 million to settle claims that customers were wrongly denied refunds for product returns. Reuters reported that Amazon, while denying any wrongdoing, will also provide other benefits as part of the settlement.

In a statement to the outlet, an Amazon spokesperson said an internal review in 2025 uncovered “a small subset of returns where we issued a refund without the payment completing, or where we could not verify that the correct item had been sent back to us, so no refund had been issued.”

Settlement administrators announced last week that while a proposed settlement has been agreed upon, it awaits court approval. The court has also not found Amazon “liable in any way,” or that the company “engaged in any wrongdoing or misconduct of any kind.”

Some have started to receive notices (which may be in your email’s spam folder) that they qualify for payment, according to posts on Reddit .

First, you need to have started a return to Amazon or asked for a refund for a product purchased on Amazon and received in the U.S. between Sept. 5, 2017, and Feb. 12, 2026. Further, you need to have either not received a refund, even though you should have, or your refund from Amazon was “untimely or incorrect,” and/or, you received a refund only to later be charged by Amazon, incorrectly, for the product or products that you were returning.

Settlement administrators explain that Amazon implemented a process to pay refunds to the customers it found were impacted as part of the aforementioned 2025 internal review. Those payments are separate from the settlement’s common fund, which Amazon is paying $309.5 million into.

After paying other costs and expenses associated with the settlement, the fund will be divided among two subclasses of class members. Members of both are “expected to receive a full refund plus interest,” but they vary in how much proof they need to provide that they qualify.

Subclass A, which will receive more than 92% of the remaining funds, according to the settlement administrators, qualify for automatic payments. These customers were impacted by “computer and payment processing errors,” court documents explained , or Amazon records showed the return wasn’t completed, “for example, because said return was potentially lost in transit.” These members will not have to file a claim but will need to identify their preferred payment option after the court approves the settlement.

Subclass B, meanwhile, will need to submit claims that show “more likely than not” that they are entitled to payment, per court documents. These customers need also to have “experienced failed refunds or retrocharges,” but Amazon’s available records “do not establish that it is more likely than not Amazon incorrectly processed the return.”

You may fall into both subclasses, but your payouts may arrive as a single payment, administrators said.

If you qualify for the settlement, you can expect to receive notification via email of your status. This will include a Notice ID and Confirmation Code that you will use to file a claim online , if you are a member of Subclass B. Paper forms are also available, but you will need to mail them in.

The form asks you to provide your contact information as well as details about the returns that were rejected or the incorrect refunds you received through Amazon. You will also need to identify your preferred payout option.

Should your claim be verified, the available options include an Amazon gift card, a check, PayPal, Venmo, Zelle, and a virtual prepaid card.

You’ll have until Dec. 1, 2026, to submit your claim.

What else should I know about this proposed settlement?

You can find more details about the settlement here .

It is still pending court approval, with a hearing scheduled for March 16, 2027. That date could move, and any appeals of the decision could delay the payout process.

Should the settlement be approved, Subclass A members will have 105 days to select their preferred payout option.

articles.title: The Trump administration needs a crash course in ‘Working Class’ from JD Vance
articles.summary: Whether the Republican leadership wants to admit it or not, they have a growing perception problem with working-class and disenfranchised Americans.
articles.body:
Note to Republican leadership: If you truly deem the Democrats coming back into power in Congress and the White House as an existential threat to our nation, then why are you handing them the winning issue for this election cycle on a silver platter?

To be sure, there are still millions of Americans who believe President Trump has an exceptional understanding of economics and that the “business of America is business.” That said, they also understand that Trump is a leader who was blessed to grow up in a bubble of wealth and privilege.

As such, the day-to-day struggles of working-class Americans, no matter how much Trump may sympathize, are still only academic to him.

Our 45th and 47th president has never experienced the hope-crushing and mentally debilitating realities millions of Americans face each waking morning. Realities such as: not having enough money to pay the rent or mortgage; the threat of eviction; being forced to choose between heating fuel or food; not having enough money to buy your child needed medicine; having to walk to your minimum wage job because you did not have enough money to buy gas for your car; not having the money to move from your crime-infested neighborhood; not having the money to fix your teeth; or not having the money so your child could attend the prom.

I can assure you, as someone who grew up in abject poverty and was homeless as a child, millions of our fellow Americans are dealing with these issues every single day. Just as I can assure you that having people in bubbles of wealth and privilege tell paycheck-to-paycheck working Americans to “suck it up” so we can prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is infuriating.

I have spoken with many Republicans and Trump supporters who have continually asked over the last few months: “Wait a minute, I thought the president said we obliterated Iran’s nuclear capability last year! So why am I now being forced to pay higher gas prices and tell my family we can no longer afford meat?”

No matter if the Republican leadership wants to admit it or not, they have a growing perception problem with working-class and disenfranchised Americans. These voters not only believe the Republicans have greatly exacerbated their daily financial struggles but are simultaneously telling them to stop whining for the good of the nation. It’s not a winning strategy in the voting booth.

Working-class Americans don’t need lectures from privileged politicians, pundits and academics. They need a champion, preferably one who lived in and escaped their world into a position of leadership, where they can actually do something about it.

Fortunately for Trump and the Republican leadership, literally right down the hall from the Oval Office sits a man who has a veritable Ph.D. in “working class American.” That person is Vice President JD Vance.

If there is one person in the Trump administration whose life story can deeply resonate with the working class of our nation, it is Vance’s. As he described in his best-selling novel “Hillbilly Elegy,” our vice president grew up a child of divorce in the Rust Belt, as his mother struggled against addiction and alcohol abuse. Vance served in the Marines and put himself through college and law school. He rose quickly in politics, from the Senate to the White House —a life story that speaks to virtually every demographic in one way or another.

In our increasingly polarized and siloed country, many Americans may have forgotten or never learned of Vance’s remarkable story. Now might be a good time for Vance to not only remind voters that he is “one of them,” but the Republican leadership as well.

Years ago, I had the honor to work in the White House for two presidents. If memory serves, there is a very nice auditorium in the Eisenhower Executive Office Building where the privileged leadership of the Trump administration can be gathered so the vice president can give them a crash course in the increasingly harsh realities faced by the working class of our nation on a daily basis.

Let’s not lecture the working class, Vance should emphasize. Let’s not speak down to them. Let’s not blame them or insult them. Rather, let us listen to them, empathize with them and seek to help them.

If the Republicans want to have any hope of not being drowned by a growing blue wave come Nov. 3, they would do tell to listen and learn.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

articles.title: Trump posts GOP senator’s cell phone number over daylight savings act stall
articles.summary: President Trump posted Sen. Tom Cotton’s (R-Ark.) cell phone number on Truth Social Saturday, lashing out at Senate Republicans to move forward with legislation that would make daylight saving time permanent. “Tom Cotton, a friend of mine, is holding up a very important Bill,” Trump wrote, describing the Sunshine Protection Act. “For some reason, Tom…
articles.body:
President Trump posted Sen. Tom Cotton’s (R-Ark.) cell phone number on Truth Social Saturday, lashing out at Senate Republicans to move forward with legislation that would make daylight saving time permanent .

“Tom Cotton, a friend of mine, is holding up a very important Bill,” Trump wrote, describing the Sunshine Protection Act. “For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it’s very easy to do, it only takes one! It should pass overwhelmingly, in a Bipartisan fashion.”

“To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate, and for America, itself. Call Tom on his cellphone,” the president continued before he wrote the number. “Let him know.”

Trump blamed Cotton for the bill — which he called the “No More Changing of Clocks Act” — stalling in the Senate after it passed the House with a 308-117 vote.

When asked about the post, Cotton’s office referred to the senator’s statement shared on social platform X , where he said, “No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter.”

“Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first,” he concluded.

Cotton, who chairs the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence , has been among the most vocal opponents of permanent daylight saving time —expressing concern that without the twice a year clock changes, many children heading to school and millions of Americans traveling to work would be left in the dark.

“If permanent daylight saving time becomes the law of the land, it will again make winter a dark and dismal time for millions of Americans,” he said last year.

Trump countered that more evening daylight would help reduce crime and traffic accidents, while benefiting public health and industries including sports, tourism, restaurants and retail.

In his Saturday Truth Social post, Trump continued that the bill would help the PGA Tour who “needs more Daylight in the afternoon in order to finish their Tournaments.”

“Likewise, regular Golfers, Tennis Players, Hunters and, perhaps most importantly, Farmers who want more Daylight to play or work,” he added.

The post included a letter from PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp who wrote in “strong support” of the bill — citing that it would generate $1 billion annually in new direct revenue for the sport.

Trump has pushed for the Sunshine Protect Act’s passage since August , but Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has cast doubt on whether the measure can secure the 60 votes needed to advance.

articles.title: Nepal’s catastrophic flooding is a red alert for the world’s mountain towns
articles.summary: Towers of ice and snow weakened by a quickly heating planet will, one way or another, wreak havoc down-mountain in vulnerable landscapes.
articles.body:
In 2011, I trekked with scientists and engineers to about 17,000 feet to look at Lake Imja in Nepal’s Everest region. I thought about that expedition from the safety of my home in Peru as I watched the awful consequences of permafrost weakened by warming upon the northern district of Rasuwa, near Nepal’s border with Tibet.

When glaciers recede, they leave an indent created by their weight. Melt from the glacier fills that bowl, growing until the pressure gets too great, or an earthquake hits. Lake Imja did not exist in 1953, when Sir Edmund Hillary conquered Everest. By 2011, it was the fastest-growing of some 1,600 glacier lakes in Nepal .

On our visit, the artificial lake stretched down from the glacier for a mile and a half, held in place by a precarious mix of debris. An earthquake or pressure on the makeshift dam could release water with disastrous consequences for vulnerable communities in Nepal.

On Aug. 26 , the world watched the consequences of a different version of what we feared. Above Rasuwa, a broken chunk of glacier, likely the size of a big New York City building, fell 4,000 feet, setting off a tsunami. Friction at that velocity melts ice. A great wave gathered ice, snow, water, rocks and mud — and then structures — to cascade down the narrow valleys, wiping out lives, communities and infrastructure. Hurricane-force winds leveled trees.

I’m safe as I write, but some version of the same can and likely will happen in my country and other mountainous regions, and again in Nepal. Towers of ice and snow weakened by a quickly heating planet will, one way or another, wreak havoc down-mountain in vulnerable landscapes.

We came back from our Lake Imja expedition shaken, but also with thoughts about how to anticipate and prepare against these disasters.

Early warning systems with real-time sensors and satellite communications can detect sudden water releases and alert downstream communities. It could help to slowly lower water levels in high-risk glacial lakes and, where possible, to future-proofing buildings and installations. Lake Imja was a slightly different situation than what happened in Rasuwa, but it carries the same danger and is more like the situation in my country.

In Peru, Palcacocha is a glacial lake in Huaraz Province . The spectacular snow-covered peaks of that part of the Andes mountain range are warming, creating the same conditions as we saw in Nepal. One hundred thousand people live below our lake, including communities and schools that inevitably will be directly in the pathway should meltwater be released and trigger a chain reaction not unlike what happened in Nepal.

Part of my job as executive director of the Instituto Andino de Montaña in Peru was to persuade the city of Huaraz to put an early warning system in place. After much effort, we achieved that. But when we tried to get officials to commit to engineering to lower the lake’s water level, we encountered red tape, indolence, wrong priorities and fear of scaring away tourists. No funding or commitment was forthcoming.

Since then, we have been holding our breath and hoping for the best. But with the ongoing El Niño event, this could be the season when our worst fears come about.

The grassroots Peruvians I work with in the countryside have no trust that government officials will protect them against these well-known risks. Huaraz is very far from Lima, our capital, and the people at risk feel invisible. Officials at the federal level are trying to pass the buck to local and private actors. But no one at the local, provincial or even regional level has the technical capacity to take on this challenging engineering work.

The U.S., where I got my Ph.D., is not immune. Melting glaciers already trigger disastrous floods and mudslides. A glacial lake outburst flood has occurred every year since 2011 at Suicide Basin, on the Mendenhall Glacier near Juneau, Alaska. The rapid retreat of the Grasshopper Glacier in Wyoming’s Wind River Mountains triggered a glacial lake outburst flood in 2003 .

American communities will suffer a quieter, less visible threat — the toxic minerals and metals from melting glaciers that leak into local water supplies, eroding life rather than blasting it away.

If disaster happens anywhere, in my country, or any number of American communities as this threat evolves, there will be official mourning. Why not invest that energy and empathy into acting now and saving lives, rather than grieving them?

Jorge Recharte Bullard Ph.D. has served as president of Instituto Andino de Montaña, the Mountain Institute’s Legacy Institution, since 2020. He was director of the Andean program of The Mountain Institute between 1997 and 2019.

articles.title: Ted Cruz slams Tucker Carlson for World War II comments
articles.summary: Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) slammed conservative commentator Tucker Carlson for a recent podcast appearance during which the former Fox News host questioned whether the United Kingdom “benefited” from its involvement in the second World War. “Yes, Tucker, the UK is better off for winning WWII,” Cruz responded to the clip in a Friday night post…
articles.body:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) slammed conservative commentator Tucker Carlson for a recent podcast appearance during which the former Fox News host questioned whether the United Kingdom “benefited” from its involvement in the second World War.

“Yes, Tucker, the UK is better off for winning WWII,” Cruz responded to the clip in a Friday night post to social platform X.

He continued, “America is better off for winning World War II. And the world would be much worse off if the Nazis had won WWII. This is not complicated.”

Carlson’s comments came during his interview with former U.K. conservative lawmaker Jacob Rees-Mogg, where the commentator made several controversial claims about WWII.

In a segment of the interview, called “Was WWII good for Britain?”, Carlson expressed doubt on whether the U.K. “won” after it helped defeat the Axis powers.

“Has the U.K. benefited from it?” Carlson asked. “There are a lot of people in Britain who can’t speak English, so it would be nice to have at least a European language spoken in your country.”

“Why don’t you tell me the ways in which Britain benefited from — I’m going to use quotes here — ‘winning the Second World War.’ Because from my perspective, it looks like the empire ended. India was lost two years later, the United States took over the world, and has had troops here ever since,” he continued.

Since Carlson’s exit from Fox News in 2023, he grown more controversial among Republican lawmakers — notably drawing ire for hosting a Holocaust revisionist on his self-titled show in 2024.

Throughout the episode, podcaster Darryl Cooper made controversial comments about Nazi Germany’s mass murder of Jewish people, claiming the genocide was a result of poor planning.

Carlson also hosted white nationalist commentator Nick Fuentes on his podcast. Fuentes has denied the Holocaust on multiple occasions and made several antisemitic remarks during his discussion with Carlson.

At the time, Cruz criticized Carlson for interviewing Fuentes, saying at the Republican Jewish Coalition Annual Summit , “If you sit there with someone who says Adolf Hitler was very cool and that their mission is to defeat ‘global Jewry,’ and you say nothing, then you are a coward, and you are complicit in that evil.”
