articles.title: Trump urges calls to Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton in push for permanent daylight saving time
articles.summary: President Donald Trump on Saturday pressured Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas to support a bill to make daylight saving time permanent, urging Americans to call w...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump on Saturday pressured Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas to support a bill to make daylight saving time permanent, urging Americans to call what appeared to be the personal cellphone number of Cotton, the chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee.

The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House in July, but it faces roadblocks in the Senate where some Republicans are strongly opposed. Proponents, including the White House, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Detractors said permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings when children will be waiting for school buses and parents will be driving to work in darkness.

It was a remarkable escalation on Trump's part of a longstanding fixation shared by both men — with Trump supporting making daylight saving time permanent, and Cotton vociferously opposed — at a time just weeks before the midterms, when Republicans would prefer that the president focus on talking about affordability issues and the party's achievements. Cotton is also up for reelection this November, although that race is not expected to be competitive.

Trump calls daylight saving time 'depressing'

Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the United States are set one hour ahead of standard time. Not all states observe it — and under the bill, states can opt out of the change if their respective legislatures act to do so before the bill's enactment.

"For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it's very easy to do, it only takes one!" Trump wrote on social media, noting that passing the bill would give professional golfers more time on the greens. "So, everyone in Arkansas, a State I love, and won 3 times, the last by by 34 points, tell Tom to, GET IT DONE! It will be appreciated by all," Trump said.

Trump included a phone number with an Arkansas area code. The Associated Press called the number, but no one answered and the voicemail box was full.

Cotton, a member of Republican leadership, reiterated his opposition to permanent daylight saving time in a social media post of his own Saturday afternoon. He is not the only GOP senator who opposes the policy, though he has been among the most vocal opponents.

"No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," Cotton wrote. "Arkansans don't want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I'll always put Arkansas first."

Trump, who is spending the day at his northern Virginia golf club before traveling to Ohio later Saturday, promptly fired back.

"If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn't have to run all over their houses, farms, work places, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so," Trump said, adding that "that is really putting Arkansas FIRST."

As his motorcade was rolling back to the White House, Trump added that "a table full of very distinguished people just told me that they HATE, immediately after a mandatory time change, going home at night – and it's DARK."

"It's depressing!" Trump continued. "One of the gentleman stated that, 'I just hate going home in darkness.' It's also, in Crime Ridden Blue States, a lot more dangerous to be walking home in the dark!"

A 2025 poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that if forced to choose, most Americans would prefer to keep that extra hour of daylight in the evening. Only 12% of U.S. adults favor the current system of daylight saving time, which requires people in most states to change their clocks twice a year, while 47% oppose it and 40% are neutral.

Members of Congress have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942. The Senate passed a bill four years ago to make daylight saving time permanent, but it stalled in the House.

This is not the first time Trump has released personal information about a senator

While competing for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina described Trump as "unfit for office" after Trump denigrated the military service of Sen. John McCain of Arizona. Trump then released Graham's personal cellphone number. That prompted a viral video in which the senator dramatically destroyed a series of flip phones.

Graham later became a close ally of Trump. In contrast, although they share many of the same policy positions, Trump and Cotton are not known to be close.

Cotton, one of the Republican Party's most prominent national security voices, has advocated for a more hawkish approach on Iran, particularly as Trump entertains pauses in military strikes amid the seven-month war. In Trump's first term, Cotton was a critic of the president's attempts at overhauling the nation's sentencing laws, calling the proposal a "jailbreak."

Earlier this year, Cotton had temporarily defied Trump's attempts at stalling the confirmation process for his own nominee for director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton. The president had wanted to ensure his interim pick for the intelligence job, Bill Pulte, would be able to serve in that role at least briefly when the former director, Tulsi Gabbard, left the job.

But the appointment of Pulte, who had no known national security credentials, drew bipartisan condemnation from Capitol Hill and Cotton had tried to expedite Clayton's confirmation process, which could have prevented Pulte from being installed as acting director.

But Trump ultimately ordered Clayton to not appear before Cotton's committee for his confirmation hearing, and Pulte served in the job for several weeks this summer. Clayton was eventually confirmed by the Senate in late July.

Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title: Breaking the tyranny of extremists
articles.summary: Political scientist Lawrence R. Jacobs argues that urgent reforms to the presidential nomination process are required to prevent the rise of populism and protect the rule of law.
articles.body:
The nearly unchecked powers of the president are controlled by the ideologues and special interests who dictate Republican nominations. Self-serving agendas take precedence over the selection of candidates with a record of abiding by the rule of law and the Constitution. Without urgent reforms, America will continue to succumb to what the Framers of the Constitution most feared — a populist tyranny.

Two consequential changes have brought us to this crossroads.

The first: Control over nominations has shifted since the 1970s. Party officials committed to winning general elections with experienced candidates gave way to relatively small and ideologically unrepresentative segments of the electorate intent on advancing their narrow agendas. The relatively low turnout for direct primaries enabled evangelicals, members of the Christian right as well as virulent opponents of immigration, abortion, taxes, and government regulation to control the delegates to national conventions who select presidential candidates.

These changes overturned the Constitution’s design to “filter” the voice of the people and insulate elected officials, especially presidents. The Electoral College, Alexander Hamilton explained in 1788 , was designed to produce “a constant probability of seeing the station filled by characters preeminent for ability and virtue” and preventing the selection of presidents inclined toward “cabal, intrigue, and corruption.”

President Trump is the nightmare. He won the 2016 nomination by scraping together less than 40 percent in early primary contests among a crowded field of opponents. As is typical of Republican primaries, three out of four voters identified as very or somewhat conservative and Trump won pluralities there. In contrast, about two-thirds of voters in the 2016 general election described themselves as moderate or liberal.

Trump’s open disregard for the rule of law and the Constitution was not a serious consideration for voters in the Republican primaries and the November general election. Nearly all Republicans robotically backed him in an era of intense party loyalty. A plurality of the remaining voters, including independents, were swayed largely by their reaction against Democrats : dislike of Hillary Clinton, opposition to the Obama administration, economic and cultural dissatisfaction and a desire for political change.

The second momentous change has been the expansion of presidential powers to act unilaterally in domestic and international affairs. Democrats and Republicans left a loaded gun in the Oval Office.

With the onset of the Cold War, presidents routinely acted alone to send troops into real or potential conflicts, conduct assassinations abroad, and reach international agreements. Extreme abuses of power were mostly skirted by the vetting of political parties and their networks. They weeded out demagogues from the pool of presidential candidates and nominated, in most cases, candidates with a track record for governing effectively.

Then came Trump — a candidate propelled to the cusp of election by narrow ideological factions without the peer review of senior elected and party officials who are attentive to the rule of law. The result: imperial power is unmoored at a time that lacks protections against unqualified and unscrupulous presidents.

Saving the republic now requires urgent reforms of the nomination process to filter out the demagogues that most worried the Constitution’s Framers. Changes are needed in both parties but most urgently in the Republican Party that lacks the informal checks from moderate donors and insiders.

A necessary starting point is to restore and expand the independence of unpledged Republican delegates: the national and state GOP leaders focused on protecting the party’s national reputation.

Until 2012, nearly a fifth of convention delegates were free to vote for any presidential candidate on the first ballot regardless of their state’s primary or caucus results. By 2016, the proportion of unpledged delegates was slashed to 6.9 percent and national and state party rules increasingly bound them to primary results.

Urgent reforms to restore balance to the Republican nomination process are possible but must be achieved soon. The party should maintain the central role of primary voters while also returning the ability of party leaders to create an off-ramp if activists favor a candidate who is a threat to rule of law and Constitution.

Ideologues will throw up a predictable smoke screen, claiming that the reforms weaken democracy. The truth is that primary voters will continue to dominate the selection of candidates. But in cases where activists are on the verge of imposing a candidate with extreme views about policy and the rule of law, party leaders must reserve a limited option to leverage their small fraction of delegates to tilt a convention toward alternatives better suited to our constitutional system and the views of most Americans.

Unless immediate and vigorous action is taken, the nomination of another vengeful and unprincipled presidential candidate is a very real possibility in 2028.

Lawrence R. Jacobs is the Walter F. and Joan Mondale Chair for Political Studies and director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota’s Humphrey School of Public Affairs. A member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, he has written or edited 19 books on American politics.

articles.title: Springsteen, other stars share stage with hardcore leftist groups at music fest
articles.summary: Bruce Springsteen and Dave Matthews headline a "Power To The People" festival featuring anti-Trump nonprofits mobilizing ahead of midterms.
articles.body: As rapper Macklemore draws controversy for his activism against Israel, rock stars Bruce Springsteen and Dave Matthews headline a "Power To The People" music festival today that features a partisan network of nonprofits and activists mobilizing against President Donald Trump ahead of the midterms. Performers from a hip-hop band, The Neighborhood Kids, launched the festival with Macklemore's anthem of protest, chanting "Free, free Palestine!" and continuing with a declaration about protesting from "the belly of the beast," against the "funding of genocide" and the "terrorist organization" Immigration and Customs Enforcement." It dedicated its performance to "the martyrs" railed against "Western imperialism." The marketing language on the "Power To The People" festival's official website speaks to activating "the power everyday human beings have" to "shape" the world "on, and beyond, Election Day." The festival bears clear signs of alignment with the Democratic Party and spotlights the intersection of pop culture, nonprofit fundraising and partisan politics, revealing how celebrity drawing power translates into money, visibility and voters for organizations advancing a political agenda. In the chat, awaiting a livestream broadcast on the Democratic-aligned MS NOW, a user wrote: "BLUE WAVE," symbolizing a anticipated Democratic Party victories in upcoming elections. Others peppered their comments with blue wave and blue heart emojis. By combining performances with voter registration, activist organizing and charitable donations, "Power To The People" offers participating groups a platform to turn fans’ enthusiasm for music into political engagement – and votes – ahead of the midterms. Festival organizers didn't respond to a request for comment. With musical artists passionately urging festival goers to vote Democratic, the event raises questions about whether participating nonprofits cross the line from permissible voter engagement into partisan campaign intervention, which federal tax law prohibits for 501(c)(3) organizations. PARTY POOPERS' FIGHT CARD: JANE FONDA, 'NO KINGS,' COMMUNISTS ROLL OUT RIVAL SPECTACLE TO TRUMP'S 250TH A "Freedom Village," set up on the festival grounds of the Merriweather Post Pavilion in Columbia, Md., outside the nation’s capital, features a roster of nonprofit organizations, including Indivisible, which is funded by billionaire George Soros, Third Act, the ACLU and other groups that have been at the heart of coordinating "No Kings," "Tesla Takedown" and "Hands Off" protests against Trump over almost two years. Last year, Springsteen performed at a "No Kings" protest at the state capitol in St. Paul, Minn., organized by Indivisible and featuring anti-Trump activist Jane Fonda. He also headlined a "No Kings" event at the Target Center in Minneapolis. FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS Many of the festival's performers and organizers bring a documented history of campaigning for Democrats and far-left activism. Festival organizer Tom Morello, guitarist of the band Rage Against the Machine, has called socialism a "necessity." Opening the concert after the hip-hop group The Neighborhood Kids, Morello blasted the "fascists and the would-be dictators" and the "oligarchs," symbolic references that protesters have used for almost two years of protests against Trump. According to an online fundraising form, the "Power To The People Festival Fund" is identified as a fiscally sponsored project of Catalyst Philanthropy Fund, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit established in 2024 in Nashville with $6.5 million in annual revenue, according to its latest tax filing. Springsteen endorsed the Democratic presidential ticket in 2024, declaring: "I’m supporting Kamala Harris for president and Tim Walz for vice president." He also called Trump "the most dangerous candidate for president in my lifetime." Artist Dave Matthews participated in the 2020 "I Will Vote" concert, which his official website promoted as supporting Biden, Harris and Democrats down the ballot. Earlier, Matthews backed socialist presidential candidate Bernie Sanders, writing: "When it comes down to it, Bernie Sanders represents what I want from my government." Artist and festival DJ Shepard Fairey created the iconic Obama "Hope" poster and the "Forward" image supporting Harris in 2024. "I believe VP Kamala Harris and her VP pick Tim Walz are our best chance to move forward," Fairey wrote on his website. He offered the image for grassroots activism and linked readers to Head Count Inc., a nonprofit receiving proceeds from the festival, to "help fans register to vote and learn more about how to participate in upcoming elections." Based in New York City, Head Count Inc. has about $14 million in revenues, according to its latest IRS tax filing. The other nonprofit receiving proceeds from the festival is VoteRiders, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit based in Washington, D.C., with $7.8 million in revenues, based on its last tax filing. The festival's "community partners" include Ben & Jerry's, the ice cream company whose co-founder Ben Cohen, a far-left activist, was a guest at the wedding of communist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham and Jodie Evans, co-founder of CodePink, a fierce anti-Trump nonprofit that has received $1.33 million from Singham. Another community partner is Red Emma's, a bookstore in Baltimore with a "Marxism, Socialism & Communism" tab on its website, selling t"Teachings of Karl Marx" by communist philosopher Vladimir Lenin, "Black Marxism" and "Flowers for Marx." The political leanings extend to younger performers. Musician "Grandson," whose real name is Jordan Benjamin, has described using his platform to advance climate advocacy, voter registration and youth empowerment through his XX Resistance Fund. In a September 2020 interview, he praised Biden’s policy platform and made his electoral preference explicit: "We should elect that dude." At the festival, he blasted "the AI apocalypse" and sang from a trademark song celebrating the self-immolation of a U.S. service member, Aaron Bushnell, in 2024 at the Embassy of Israel in Washington, D.C., protesting Israel's military response to the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas. "Martyrdom is meditation, self-immolation!" the musician sang, bouncing on stage. At "Power to the People," the concept of "solidarity" comes with a VIP upgrade. The festival pairs its message of collective action with a familiar concert-business model: tiered admission, exclusive viewing areas and premium hospitality. Fans can choose between "People’s Park" lawn admission, "People’s Pavilion" access and the "Solidarity Circle" VIP package, which offers reserved seating, expedited entry and an "exclusive VIP deck with premium bar and food available for purchase." The top-tier "Robinhood Package," branded a "VIP SUPER SUITE," adds an exclusive suite, a dedicated viewing area at the second stage and an elevated balcony advertised as offering "the very best view of the stage and the festival." Buyers also receive a commemorative poster and laminate, a phone-charging station and a "VIP host with concierge service for bar/food available for purchase." Even at the highest tier, the advertised refreshments cost extra. Organizers say the premium packages serve a charitable purpose, but the website uses differing descriptions of the donation pledge. Its overview promises a portion of all ticket proceeds and "100% of the net proceeds from VIP tickets" to VoteRiders and Head Count. The package descriptions instead promise "all proceeds from VIP sales" to nonprofits supporting human rights and social justice. The commercial offerings extend beyond the venue. The festival’s website promotes a paid membership with its livestream partner, MS NOW, advertising access to "daily live interactions and Q&As" with personalities including Democratic-aligned hosts Rachel Maddow, Jen Psaki, Al Sharpton and Joe Scarborough and Jen Psaki, a former Biden spokeswoman. Alongside calls for "grassroots organizing" and "mutual aid," the event offers a marketplace of upgraded access, media subscriptions and "hospitality." Back on stage with the Neighborhood Kids, the hip-hop artists continued their blast of ICE and pumped their fists in the air to inspire the concertgoers. "Power to the people!" they shouted. "Rest in peace to all the martyrs," one member of the group yelled. "Free the world! Free Palestine! Free Congo! Free Armenia! Free Sudan! And free everywhere in the world from Western imperialism." "And we got merch in that tent!" the member of the group continued, pointing toward the "Freedom Village," as another yelled "¡Viva la revolución!" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

articles.summary: Rep. Randy Fine discusses the rationale for backing the conflict in Iran, explains the meaning of an America First foreign policy, and denounces Rep. Ilhan Omar on immigration fraud
articles.body: MAGA firebrand Congressman Randy Fine, R-Fla., warned the U.S. must stop Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons as he cautioned America is losing the battle against radical Islam. MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD-LINKED NETWORKS EMBEDDED ACROSS CANADIAN INSTITUTIONS, NEW REPORT ALLEGES He continued, "And I think they're hoping that the American pressure, both military and economic, will cause the regime to either restructure or collapse. I certainly would like to see them stand up for themselves and overthrow the mainstream Muslim religious leaders that are in charge there." Following the IRGC's recent call to the American electorate to oppose Donald Trump in the midterm elections, Fine said that the move has the potential to impact the ballot box. "Well, I hope it does. And I personally believe the conflict would have been over a long time ago if it wasn't for Democrats supporting the enemy," he said. "See, the mainstream Muslim religious leaders in Iran can see that Democrats aren't on board. And they say, ‘hey, maybe we can wait out Donald Trump and the Republicans and get that nuclear weapon that we want to use in the United States.’ So, I'm not surprised." TURKEY’S NATO ROLE UNDER SCRUTINY AMID NEW REPORT ON HAMAS, MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD TIES "I don't think it should be an explicit goal of American foreign policy. I think it probably happens as a result. But I'm an America First guy. And if crazy people want to run Iran, that's not America's problem unless they threaten America. And that's what they have done." He said, "For 47 years, the mainstream Muslim religious leaders who've run Iran have said 'death to America.' They've killed thousands of Americans. They're trying to build missiles that can reach America. They're trying to build a nuclear weapon that can reach America, so stopping that is in our interest." He added, "But if they said, 'look America's our friend, we're going to leave you alone' well then it's not an America First problem anymore. We're not the world's policeman, but we have to look out for America's interests and making sure Iran can't nuke us: that's about as America First as it gets." However, given the prospect of Iran obtaining a nuclear weapon, Fine's answer modulates. "I mean, the answer is they can't have a nuclear weapon. articles.title: Tennessee prison chief resigns after failed execution as former US attorney tapped to lead independent review
articles.summary: Frank Strada resigned as Tennessee's corrections commissioner after Christa Pike's botched lethal injection left her hospitalized on a ventilator.
articles.body: The head of Tennessee's prison system is resigning after the state's failed lethal injection of convicted murderer Christa Pike left her hospitalized and on a ventilator. Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada will step down this month, Gov. Bill Lee said Saturday. In a statement distributed by the governor's office, Strada said stepping aside was "in the best interest of Tennesseans" while an independent review examines what went wrong during the botched execution. "I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred," Strada said. DEATH ROW INMATE UNCONSCIOUS ON VENTILATOR AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION FOR TEEN’S KILLING: ATTORNEYS At Lee's request, the Tennessee Attorney General's Office has retained former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton to conduct an independent review of the correction department's actions in carrying out Pike's court-ordered sentence, the state announced Saturday. The review will examine the state Department of Correction's actions in carrying out Pike's court-ordered sentence, including whether the state's execution protocol was followed and whether additional recommendations are needed. Lee also called off the remaining execution scheduled in Tennessee this year pending completion of the review. Stanton previously conducted an independent review of Tennessee's lethal injection protocol in 2022. His work prompted the state and Attorney General's Office to substantially rewrite the protocol before executions resumed. Lee said Strada served with integrity, adding that he appreciates his "willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment." "I have accepted his decision to step down and am grateful for his commitment to ensuring a smooth leadership transition," Lee said. CHRISTA PIKE’S BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTION TAKES FOCUS OFF VICTIM, JEOPARDIZES EXECUTION: FORMER POLICE CHIEF Pike, 50, was injected with two doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday night, and prison officials used at least seven needles while trying to find a vein. Pike was heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly during the execution, according to a Friday court filing from her lawyers. She was taken to the hospital, where she had to be intubated and put on a ventilator, her lawyers said. In a statement obtained by The Associated Press, Pike's four-person legal team celebrated the departure of Strada but said it wasn't enough. "What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," they said. "We hope the governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system." Her lawyers said in the court filing that the prison staff did not correctly place the IV lines. They also claimed staff failed to realize that one of Pike's veins burst, leading to at least some of the pentobarbital entering her body. DEATH ROW INMATE TONY CARRUTHERS WON'T FACE EXECUTION FOR AT LEAST A YEAR AFTER IV LINE FAILURE IN TENNESSEE Strada became commissioner of Tennessee's correction department in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections. In late 2024, he announced that Tennessee would solely use pentobarbital as its execution drug. Four people have been executed in Tennessee since last year, according to the department. On the evening of Jan. 12, 1995, Christa Pike, then 18, lured 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer into a wooded area near the University of Tennessee's agricultural campus. Pike and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, then spent 30 minutes torturing Slemmer, while 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson served as a lookout. According to her confession to authorities, Pike killed Slemmer because she believed she was interested in her boyfriend romantically. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Even though Shipp directly participated in the murder, he was ineligible for the death penalty because he was 17 at the time. He was sentenced to life in prison with parole, which he has not yet received. Peterson, who cooperated with investigators and testified against Pike and Shipp, was given 460 days in jail after pleading guilty to being an accessory. Pike was the only one in the case sentenced to death and became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row. She would have been the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump appears to post Sen. Tom Cotton’s cell number in push to make daylight saving time permanent
articles.summary: President Donald Trump on Saturday appeared to share Sen. Tom Cotton’s cellphone number in a social media post amid a push to make daylight saving time permanent nationwide.
articles.body: President Donald Trump on Saturday appeared to share Sen. Tom Cotton’s cellphone number in a social media post amid a push to pass the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent nationwide. “Republicans in the Senate have to get moving on what I call the ‘No More Changing of Clocks Act,’ officially known as The Sunshine Protection Act,” the president wrote in a post on Truth Social early Friday morning. In that post, he said the twice-annual American tradition of changing the clocks “costs our Country a fortune, is bad for Crime, stress on people, Sports, and just about everything else you can imagine.” On Saturday, in a separate Truth Social post, Trump wrote of Cotton, an Arkansas Republican: “Everybody in Arkansas, Tom Cotton, a friend of mine, is holding up a very important Bill. It’s called, ‘The Sunshine Protection Act’ or, ‘We Don’t Want to Change Our Clocks Twice a Year Act.’” “For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it’s very easy to do, it only takes one! It should pass overwhelmingly, in a Bipartisan fashion,” he added. In Saturday’s post, the president also appeared to include the senator’s phone number, writing: “To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate, and for America, itself. Call Tom on his cellphone ... and let him know.” Trump posted about Cotton for a third time later Saturday, writing, “If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn’t have to run all over their houses, farms, work places, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so.” A spokesperson for Cotton’s office directed NBC News to a post on X from the senator on Saturday, where he wrote, “No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter. Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first.” The senator has previously opposed establishing permanent daylight saving time, saying dark winter mornings negatively affect Americans’ health and well-being. Cotton has pointed to the 1970s, when Congress did institute permanent daylight saving time but eventually reversed course after public opinion on it tanked. “It’s said that those who don’t learn from history are doomed to repeat it. And that’s what would happen if Congress passes the so-called Sunshine Protection Act, once again ending Standard Time and imposing daylight savings time year-round,” Cotton said in a 2025 floor speech. “If permanent daylight savings time becomes the law of the land, it will again make winter a dark and dismal time for millions of Americans,” he added. “By moving the clock back an hour in winter, permanent daylight savings time would push winter sunrises to an absurdly late hour, depriving Americans of morning sunshine that’s essential for our safety and well-being.” The House passed the bill in July, with a bipartisan vote, sending it over to the Senate, which hasn’t yet taken up the measure. In 2022, the Senate was the chamber to lead on the issue, passing an earlier version of the Sunshine Protection Act that would have made daylight saving time permanent. The bill that year was co-sponsored by a bipartisan group of senators including Sens. James Lankford, R-Okla., Ron Wyden, D-Ore., Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., Rick Scott, R-Fla., Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., and Ed Markey, D-Mass. Following his election to a second term in 2024, Trump pledged to make eliminating the need to change clocks twice a year a key part of his policy agenda. In December of that year, several weeks before his inauguration, Trump wrote on Truth Social that “the Republican Party will use its best efforts to eliminate Daylight Saving Time, which has a small but strong constituency, but shouldn’t! Daylight Saving Time is inconvenient, and very costly to our Nation.” In his posts Friday and Saturday, Trump also highlighted support for the “Sunshine Protection Act” from Brian Rolapp, the CEO of the PGA Tour. “Even the highly respected PGA Commissioner, Brian Rolapp, needs it for the completion of Golf Tournaments in the Winter, when they just plain run out of sunlight,” the president wrote on Friday.

articles.title: Trump drops Republican Senator's phone number in social post over fury on stalled bill
articles.summary: President Donald Trump posted Tom Cotton's alleged cell phone number on Truth Social, urging Arkansas voters to pressure him on daylight saving time.
articles.body: President Donald Trump appeared to share the personal cell phone number of Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., on Truth Social amid his push to pass a bill which would end daylight's savings time. Trump called out Cotton, who he describes as "a friend," for stopping the "Sunshine Protection Act" from going to a vote last October. "For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it’s very easy to do, it only takes one! It should pass overwhelmingly, in a Bipartisan fashion," Trump posted on Truth Social. "So, everyone in Arkansas, a State I love, and won 3 times, the last by by 34 points, tell Tom to, GET IT DONE!" TRUMP URGES SENATE TO PASS BILL MAKING DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME PERMANENT AFTER OVERWHELMING HOUSE VOTE At the end of his post, Trump prompted Arkansas voters to call Cotton's number, which he included. Fox News Digital called the phone number associated with the Dardanelle, Arkansas, area code but did not reach Cotton. The Truth Social post from Trump comes as the Senate is out of session until Nov. 3 and unable to vote on the bill until after the midterm elections. The House passed its version of the bill in July by 308–117, garnering bipartisan support. The House bill was referred to a Senate committee, but it hasn't been touched. HOUSE PASSES DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME REFORM AS TRUMP SIGNALS SUPPORT FOR ENDING CLOCK CHANGE Trump has been a leading advocate of ending the twice-yearly clock change, arguing that it would help "decrease Robbery and Murder Rates, Reduce Car Accidents (especially those involving Pedestrians!), Lower Risk for Cardiac Issues, Stroke, and Seasonal Depression," among a laundry list of other benefits of having an extra hour of daylight in the evening. But the bill’s failure to pass despite bipartisan support marks another setback for Trump, who has made the SAVE America Act a priority but has been unable to get it signed into law. TRUMP FACES REPUBLICAN REBELLION OVER DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME AS SENATE BILL NEARS DEAD END Hours after Trump called out Cotton for rejecting a bipartisan unanimous consent made by Sens. Rick Scott, R-Fla., Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I. and Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala. to move the Senate bill last Fall, the Arkansas senator doubled down on his support for daylight savings time. "No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," Cotton psoted on X. "Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first." This isn’t the first time Trump has publicly disclosed a lawmaker’s cellphone number. In 2015, while campaigning for president, Trump shared the number of then-Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., at a rally in South Carolina. The move came after Graham called Trump a "jackass" on CBS that morning. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: White House defends media outlet bans, now citing ‘professionalism’ standards
articles.summary: Trump administration lawyers are fighting back against CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s attempt to prevent the White House from enforcing futures bans against them — with the Justice Department (DOJ) now arguing the three outlets failed to meet “professional” standards. “The President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and…
articles.body:
Trump administration lawyers are fighting back against CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s attempt to prevent the White House from enforcing futures bans against them — with the Justice Department (DOJ) now arguing the three outlets failed to meet “professional” standards.

“The President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information,’” the DOJ attorneys representing President Trump wrote in a Friday night court filing .

The filing comes as Trump continues his efforts to restrict these networks’ coverage of him despite a federal judge ruling against a previous White House grounds ban. Most recently, the administration prevented CNN from fulfilling two previously scheduled television press pool duties, barring its reporters from traveling with the president.

The Friday filing cites Truth Social posts from the president in the days following the ban , where Trump wrote that “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press,” but rather “instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS.”

The DOJ legal team reupped its claims that CNN, MS NOW and Politico jeopardized national security by “publishing classified” information, with the department now adding they believe their reporting on the administration demonstrates these networks “have failed to maintain minimum professional journalistic standards.”

The filing also argued that, throughout history, presidents have “have long decided which journalists should receive privileged access, which has varied substantially from administration to administration” — including George Washington handpicking journalists “based on political considerations” for his Farewell Address.

Trump initially banned the outlets in September, with TV “pool,” as it is known — consisting of CNN, Fox News, ABC, NBC and CBS — issuing a statement blasting the president’s move to keep CNN from the White House. The group then held back coverage of the president for days in solidarity with the cable channel.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the White House violated the media companies’ due process rights, and access for journalists working for the three outlets was restored.

The DOJ has sought to reinstate the ban, with senior counsel Michael Velchik writing in a past court filing, “After all, access to the White House is a privilege — not a right.”

Attorney General Todd Blanche also said on Sunday that “the president hasn’t denied access” to the outlets.

“That’s not the right way to describe it. This is what the president has said –– is that he is sick and tired of certain media outlets just refusing to report accurate news,” he said.

The Trump administration now faces a new fight over the White House preventing CNN reporters from fulfilling their press pool duties for his trip to Knoxville for Tennessee-Texas college football game, as well as campaign events in Oklahoma and Texas.

articles.title: Trump, Cotton tussle over daylight savings after cell phone number leak
articles.summary: President Trump repeatedly berated Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) on Saturday over his stance on a daylight savings bill after posting the Republican Congress member’s cell phone number on social media. In a morning Truth Social post, the president encouraged his supporters to call the senator and urge him to back legislation that would make daylight…
articles.body:
President Trump repeatedly berated Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) on Saturday over his stance on a daylight savings bill after posting the Republican Congress member’s cell phone number on social media.

In a morning Truth Social post , the president encouraged his supporters to call the senator and urge him to back legislation that would make daylight savings time the permanent standard time. After Cotton stood by his position in a brief statement shared later Saturday, which didn’t directly mention the president or the leak, Trump went back on the offensive.

“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” Cotton’s post read. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first.”

Trump responded on Truth Social, “If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn’t have to run all over their houses, farms, work places, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so.”

“That is really putting Arkansas FIRST, and I know, because, unlike Tom, I won that Great State, three times, and by almost 40 points!” the president continued.

The president has repeatedly pushed Congress to pass the Sunshine Protection Act of 2025, claiming in his post that the move would decrease the national crime rate because “CRIMINALS DON’T LIKE WORKING IN THE LIGHT.”

In his first post targeting Cotton, who chairs the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence , Trump blamed the GOP lawmaker for holding up the bill in the upper chamber after the House passed the legislation in July with broad bipartisan support.

“To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate, and for America, itself. Call Tom on his cellphone,” the president wrote before sharing Cotton’s number. “Let him know.”

In one of two follow-up post on Saturday afternoon, the president pushed back on the senator’s resistance to changing his position on this bill and called Cotton’s stance “ego” driven.

Trump wrote in his other post that “a table full of very distinguished people” told him “they HATE” going home at night in the dark after the daylight savings time change.

“It’s depressing! One of the gentleman stated that, ‘I just hate going home in darkness,’” the president wrote. “It’s also, in Crime Ridden Blue States, a lot more dangerous to be walking home in the dark!”

As of 4 p.m. on Saturday, Cotton has not responded to Trump’s second and third Truth Social posts against him. The Hill has reached out to the Arkansas senator and the White House for comment.

articles.title: Sunday shows preview: Trump boosts midterm candidates in final stretch; Supreme Court opens new term
articles.summary: With a month until the midterm elections, President Trump is hitting the campaign trail in an effort to ramp up voter turnout across traditionally red states, as rising costs and a deeply unpopular Iran war leave the GOP scrambling to protect its majority in Congress. Trump’s October campaign blitz will feature stops in Oklahoma, Alabama,…
articles.body:
With a month until the midterm elections, President Trump is hitting the campaign trail in an effort to ramp up voter turnout across traditionally red states, as rising costs and a deeply unpopular Iran war leave the GOP scrambling to protect its majority in Congress.

Trump’s October campaign blitz will feature stops in Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio, Texas and Nebraska — Republican-friendly states that he comfortably won in 2024. The stops are part of the party’s strategy to replicate Trump’s 2024 success and voter turnout as the party grapples with Trump’s souring approval ratings ahead of November.

Several toss-up races have moved towards Democrats, indicating potential success for the party in November. The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report last week shifted the Senate races in Kansas and South Carolina towards Democrats, while 10 GOP House seats are now looking more likely to flip.

Vice President Vance is also hitting the campaign trail, with plans to head to Alaska for a midterm rally amid the red state’s highly competitive Senate race.

The campaign push comes as Republicans contend with voter concerns over the economy and the ongoing war with Iran, which has caused energy prices to surge and has become a point of tension for some GOP candidates.

Senate nominee Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) publicly broke from Trump over the conflict, saying Iowans “shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran.”

Trump, meanwhile, has increasingly tied the end of the war and economic relief to the election. While he has floated a prediction that the conflict will end after the November elections, he told reporters at a campaign rally in Oklahoma that he thinks it’s possible the war could cost him the midterm elections.

The Supreme Court is also taking center stage as the justices prepare to begin a new term Monday, with major cases involving immigration, gun rights, voting and religious freedom on the docket.

Justice Samuel Alito will make a rare Sunday show appearance this weekend on “Fox News Sunday” alongside Attorney General Todd Blanche.

Immigration is poised to remain a major issue before the justices, with prominent challenges to the Trump administration’s policies among the cases the court has agreed to hear, including the legality of Trump’s mandatory detention policy .

In a major expansion of the government’s immigration powers, the administration argues it can lawfully detain individuals without bond if they are found to have entered the country unlawfully, even if they have lived on U.S. soil for years.

The Trump administration also made a major push on artificial intelligence this week, with the president signing an executive order alongside leading tech executives focused on the development of AI and renaming it “superintelligence.”

As part of a series of other AI initiatives, the administration launched America.gov , an AI-powered portal intended to streamline access to federal services.

Executives from technology giants, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and xAI founder Elon Musk, all made a voluntary pledge outlining commitments surrounding the development of the advanced technology. Trump described the agreement as “morally binding.”

Elsewhere, a high-profile sexual assault investigation at Cornell University and Tennessee’s botched attempt to execute convicted murderer Christa Pike have dominated headlines.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to investigate allegations that a 20-year-old Cornell student, labeled Jane Doe, was drugged and gang raped by seven men at a fraternity house in 2024.

The case has drawn renewed national attention following a civil lawsuit and questions surrounding the initial investigation, which concluded without criminal charges. Thomas Guiffra, an attorney representing the Cornell Jane Doe, will appear on CNN’s “State of the Union” this Sunday.

Meanwhile, Tennessee officials are facing scrutiny following two failed lethal injection attempts that have left death row inmate Pike is currently on life support and in critical condition.

Pike was convicted of first-degree murder in 1996 after admitting to murdering her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp.

The botched execution attempts prompted Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) to halt the state’s remaining executions for the year and order an independent investigation.

NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday”: Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.).

CBS News’s “Face the Nation”: Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.).

CNN’s “State of the Union”: National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett, Thomas Giuffra.

Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday”: Attorney General Todd Blanche, Justice Samuel Alito.

NBC News’s “Meet the Press”: Rahm Emanuel, Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), Steve Kornacki.

Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures”: National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett, Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.), Miranda Devine, Ben Domenech, Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.).
